newsitem.title: IRAQ: Turkish army pursues elusive PKK in northern Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Turkish army pursues elusive PKK in northern Iraq.

text.p: Turkish forces solidified their hold on northern Iraq on Friday, reopening the border to deliveries of humanitarian aid even as they pounded rebel Kurdish positions for the third day running.

Air force planes flew dozens of bombing runs from Turkish bases against suspected camps of the separatist Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), which is waging a 12-year insurgency for autonomy or independence from Turkey.
Military officials in Diyarbakir, headquarters for the anti-PKK fight, said heavy fighting was continuing in the Sinaht Valley, east of the main Iraqi border town of Zakho.
They said one member of Turkey's Kurdish militia was killed and four were wounded in the clashes. State-paid village guards from the southeast often join the army on operations in Iraq.
However, the anti-Baghdad Iraqi National Congress told Reuters their contacts in the region indicated most of the PKK rebels had fled south, well out of range of Turkish patrols.
"We are now sure that PKK forces have crossed over into Iraqi government-controlled territory at Shekan," said an INC spokesman in London, citing satellite telephone links to Iraq.
Other PKK units had crossed into Iran, INC said.
Turkish forces were now setting up command centres and appeared to be preparing for a lengthy stay, the INC said.

In a sign of growing confidence, the army reopened the border, closed since just before the attack, to deliveries of food and other supplies under United Nations auspices. Traders with Iraqi passports were also permitted to pass.
"We have been waiting for three days -- we are 10,000 trucks -- but now we are expecting to cross," said one lorry driver at the border. Many trucks had already crossed.
"We are going to let in traders with Iraqi passports and United Nations trucks with humanitarian supplies," a colonel at the border told reporters.

Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, an early advocate of a political solution to the PKK insurgency, said the army had been invited in to help the biggest Iraqi Kurdish group in its own fight with the PKK. The Iraqi Kurds have yet to confirm this.

"One of the most important leaders in northern Iraq...called upon our help while engaging in clashes with terrorist forces," he said. "Turkey is always respectful of Iraq's territorial integrity. This is a limited operation."
In Brussels, a PKK representative called on the Kurdish diaspora to prepare for war against Turkey.

"Our citizens in the West must respond to the call for mobilisation," Dogan Cudi of the Front for the National Liberation of Kurdistan, a wing of the PKK, told a news conference. "Our people must be ready, if necessary, for war."
Cudi said the Turkish attack was indiscriminate, hitting Iraqi Kurdish civilians as well as targeting guerrillas.

The incursion -- the biggest in two years and involving at least 10,000 troops -- has been carried out under a complete "news blackout", with reporters barred from the area and calls blocked from Turkey to satellite telephones inside Iraq.
Independent confirmation of casualty reports, as well as the full scope of operations, was impossible.
The PKK's Cudi put the death toll at eight soldiers and eight state militia members, with no PKK casualties.
Earlier, the general staff said 87 PKK rebels had been killed in Turkey's border provinces of Sirnak and Hakkari as they fled the Turkish advance from positions inside Iraq.
